paragraphs.text: Why 7.7 billion people depend on air-made fertilizer.
Start with the assumption. Harvests would fall far below what today's population needs.
That is the first effect — but not the biggest. Assume the world lost synthetic nitrogen fertilizer.

The second-order effect is stranger. Why 7.7 billion people depend on air-made fertilizer. The Haber process pulls nitrogen from the air. Air is about 78% nitrogen, but it barely reacts. Each pass converts only about 15% into ammonia. Recycling the gases eventually reaches 97% conversion. It uses 3 to 5% of the world's natural gas. Without it, today's harvests couldn't feed today's population. So much of the food on your plate began as air. The Haber process enabled the global population to increase from 1.6 billion in 1900 to 7.7 billion by November 2018. Although atmospheric nitrogen (N2) is abundant, comprising ~78% of the air, it is exceptionally stable and does not readily react with other chemicals. On each pass, only about 15% conversion occurs; due to the recycling of leftover reactants, eventually conversion of 97% is achieved. The Haber process consumes 3–5% of the world's natural gas production (around 1–2% of the world's energy supply). The Haber process fixes atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia, the basis of most nitrogen fertilizer. The world lost synthetic nitrogen fertilizer.
And here is where science stops being certain. The governing physics: the Haber process fixes atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia, the basis of most nitrogen fertilizer.
So what is the answer? The exact timeline depends on how the impossible change happens; the order of effects is what established physics constrains.
